hero.title: Helping Auckland audiences get closer to TEDx
hero.intro: TEDxAuckland is an independently run TED event. I volunteered to redesign its website, and what started as leading the design turned into running the whole project, with a team of four over about six months.

image.alt: The TEDxAuckland homepage in a browser window, over a dark photo of the event venue

facts.v: Volunteer, leading the design and the project

sections.heading: Starting from a site that only just worked

p: The previous year's site had been built in CloudCannon by another volunteer, and by the time I first looked at it, it was broken in enough places to be a real problem. It still loaded, but the most important part was missing.

blocks.text: There was no clear way to buy a ticket, which for an event website is most of what it needs to do.

p: The organisation needed the new site to reflect the energy of its events, let people book tickets online, and bring its speakers to a wide local audience.

sections.heading: Making talks, speakers and tickets easy to find

blocks.title: Built to be scanned
p: I broke the content into clear sections with a strong hierarchy, so each page reads as a series of short blocks with clear headings and generous spacing rather than long paragraphs. The same content modules are reused from page to page.

image.alt: Four talk cards from the Talks page, each with a photo, title, speaker name and topic tags
image.caption: Every talk card uses the same module, with a photo, title, speaker and topic tags.

blocks.title: Simpler navigation
p: I wanted the speakers, the schedule and the ticket link to be easy to find without anyone having to dig through dense content.
Buy ticket sits at the right of the menu on every page, and a red strip under each page header shows the next event, its date and the venue.

image.alt: Top of the TEDxAuckland homepage: menu, Buy ticket link, hero and the red upcoming event strip
image.caption: The menu, the ticket link and the next event are all visible before anyone scrolls.

blocks.title: Speakers at the centre
p: Speakers are one of the main reasons people come to TEDx events, so the speaker section needed to work especially well. Choosing a speaker opens their bio, links and talk right there in the grid, which lets people look through the line-up without leaving the page.

image.alt: A speaker selected in the grid, with her bio, links and talk video opened below
image.caption: Speaker details open inside the grid, and each portrait fades from black and white to colour when it is selected.

blocks.title: More than one way in
p: The homepage offers several starting points. People can browse by speaker, by topic and theme, or through previous talks, so they can begin with whatever interests them most rather than being led down a single path to the ticket page.

image.alt: The most popular talks banner and the talk filter, with Popular, Category and Years tabs and hashtag topics
image.caption: Talks can be filtered by popularity, category, year or topic.

p: I kept the palette close to the TED brand, with black and charcoal backgrounds, white type, and one red kept for actions and event details. Main headings are set in Noe Display Bold and subheadings in Gotham Bold.

Because the event's visuals, from the logo to the stage and its lighting, are built on a strong contrast between red and black, we decided to keep the whole website dark, apart from the blog, which uses a light background for readability. That kept the site consistent with the feel of the event itself.

The speaker thumbnails also have a spotlight effect that slowly changes each photo from black and white to colour. It mirrors the way speakers appear on stage, and it is a small touch that makes browsing the line-up a little more interesting.

blocks.title: Home and talks
blocks.alt: The rest of the TEDxAuckland homepage, with talks and upcoming events, and the Talks page
blocks.caption: The homepage moves from speakers to talks and then to upcoming events, and the Talks page opens on the most popular talks.

blocks.title: People and speakers
blocks.alt: The People page and a speaker page with bio, links and the talk video
blocks.caption: Each speaker also has a page of their own, with their bio, links and the talk they gave.

blocks.title: Partners
blocks.alt: The Partners page with a grid of partner logos
blocks.caption: The Partners page lists the event's partners, along with a short note for organisations that would like to get involved.

p: Selling tickets directly through the site became complicated quickly. With four volunteers, we did not have the time or resource to build it properly, so ticketing moved to Ticketmaster.
The site still takes people through most of the process before they buy, from learning about the event and browsing speakers and topics to understanding what the ticket includes.

blocks.text: Only the final step happens somewhere else, and everything leading up to it stays on the TEDxAuckland site.

sections.heading: Nobody had said who was doing what

p: Before this project, I had only worked in agencies, where everyone knows their role and the work moves along without anyone having to ask. The producer was not used to working that way and assumed I would take care of everything, so for a while things stood still until I noticed they had.

What changed it was a meeting where I explained plainly what was missing and where we needed to get to. From then on we had regular meetings, a timeline and deadlines, and once everyone could see the whole project and their own part in it, the work started to move.

blocks.text: Looking back, the most useful lesson from this project had very little to do with design.

p: On a volunteer team, nobody is anyone's boss and every deadline is optional, so someone has to say clearly who is doing what, and by when. That was my job, and it took me longer than it should have to realise it.
